Learn step by step

This lesson builds the whole story of this page one idea at a time, in 39 short steps in 7 chapters: the channel and one step of its physics, rewards and values, the recorded data and what the main test removed from it, how the learner learns from recorded rows a critic (a learned estimate of how good each command is) and an actor (the controller the critic trains), and where its critic goes wrong, how Bayesian Conformal Aggregation (BCA) puts a band around the critic's value that should hold its error a stated share of the time, how that band is used, and what the tests found. It follows one real moment of the channel, start 0, and one real recorded row, row 209, from start to finish, with the real numbers.

Each step states its goal, explains one idea in a few plain sentences, gives the rule as a formula with a key to its symbols, and then works the rule out with real numbers, line by line. A line shows “=” only when the numbers as shown give the result as shown, and “≈” when rounding makes them differ in the last digit; tap a line to see the full values and where they come from. Then you can try the rule yourself with a small control and check yourself with one question.

Move with Next and Previous at the end of each step, or jump to any step in this list. The page remembers the last step you read and marks the steps you have visited. (The lesson's steps are numbered 1.1 to 7.3; a step of the channel is one tick of its clock, step 1.1.)

Chapter 1. The channel, one step at a time

Meet the channel through one real moment, start 0, and work out by hand what one step does to it.

Chapter 1 · Step 1 of 39

1.1 The channel and its parts

Goal: Know what is in the channel and which 13 numbers describe it at one moment.

ThrusterChain is a small simulated water channel with five floats in a row; springs hold each float near its resting place, so a float that is pushed away swings back and forth, and the swing slowly fades.

Water flows past the floats: a steady current, plus waves that rise and fall, pushes every float downstream.

Four thrusters sit between neighboring floats; a controller sets them to keep the floats near rest without wasting throttle.

The channel moves in steps, like the ticks of a clock: at each step the controller sets the thrusters once, and every number that describes the channel changes once (step 1.9 works one step out).

Each float needs two numbers, the current needs one and the wave two, so 13 numbers describe the whole channel at one moment.

The rule

Five floats with two numbers each, one number for the current and two for the wave make 13 numbers.

What the symbols mean

What the symbols mean

5 × 2
the five floats, two numbers each: a position number and a speed number
1
the current: one number
2
the wave: two numbers

With the numbers

float numbers= 5 × 2 = 10
all numbers= 10 + 1 + 2 = 13
The code lists them in this order: p₁, v₁, p₂, v₂, p₃, v₃, p₄, v₄, p₅, v₅, c, w₁, w₂ (13 labels); there are 4 thrusters.

Chapter 1 · Step 2 of 39

1.2 Start 0: the 13 numbers

Goal: Read a real state and measure how far each float is from rest.

A float's two numbers are its position number p and its speed number v; both are 0 when the float is at rest.

Think of them as a point on a small map whose center is rest: p and v work like a position and a speed, and as the float swings, its point circles the center.

The float's distance from rest is the length of the line from the center to that point.

This lesson follows one real moment from start to finish: start 0, the first of the 1,000 fixed starting states of the evaluation bank, on which the project tests every controller (the page numbers them from 0, as in its live panel's "start 11").

The rule

The state x is the ten float numbers s, then the current c, then the two wave numbers.

Chapter 1 · Step 3 of 39

1.3 Four throttles, and clipping

Goal: Read a command of four throttles and know what clipping does.

A command sets the four thrusters' throttles, one number each: a = (a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄), each from −1 to 1.

A negative throttle pushes upstream, against the water; a positive one pushes downstream, with it; 0 is off.

A number asked for outside −1 to 1 is first cut back to the nearest end: this is called clipping.

This chapter follows one real command: the one given at start 0 by the controller that made the project's recorded data (step 3.1 shows how it chose it).

The rule

A command is four throttles, one per thruster.

What the symbols mean

What the symbols mean

a = (a1, …, a4)
the command: four throttles, one per thruster, each from −1 to 1; a negative throttle pushes upstream
ak, k
thruster k's throttle, for k = 1 to 4

Clipping keeps a number inside −1 to 1.

What the symbols mean

What the symbols mean

clip(·, −1, 1)
cut a number back to the nearest end of −1 to 1 when it lies outside
ak, k
thruster k's throttle, for k = 1 to 4
min, max
the smaller and the larger of the numbers in the parentheses

Also new in this step

|a|
the size of a throttle, without its sign (0.8 means 80%)

With the numbers

The chapter's command: a = (−0.9896, −0.2072, −0.5951, −0.4267).
clip(−0.9896, −1, 1) = −0.9896: it is already inside, so nothing changes.
A request of −1.3 would become clip(−1.3, −1, 1) = −1 (an example input, not a recorded number).
thruster 1:0.9896 × 100 = 98.96 (so 98.96% upstream; the minus sign means upstream)

Chapter 1 · Step 4 of 39

1.4 The push, and the stall past 80%

Goal: Turn a throttle into the push it really gives, including the stall.

Up to 80% throttle (|a| at most 0.8), a thruster's push equals its throttle.

Past 80% the propeller stalls: each extra unit of throttle loses 1.5 units of push, so 90% pushes only 0.65 and full throttle only 0.5.

The push keeps the throttle's direction; only its strength drops.

This is the stalling world, where the project's data were recorded. The page also uses a no-stall comparison world: the same channel, with the push always equal to the throttle.

The rule

The push f(a) equals the throttle up to 80%; past 80% its size falls by 1.5 for each unit of extra throttle.

What the symbols mean

What the symbols mean

|a|
the size of a throttle, without its sign: 0.8 means 80%
f(a)
the push a thruster really gives at throttle a

The push keeps the throttle's direction.

What the symbols mean

What the symbols mean

sign(a)
+1 or −1: the direction of a
f(a)
the push a thruster really gives at throttle a

Also new in this step

stalling world
the channel with the stall: the world the data were recorded in
no-stall comparison world
the same channel with the push always equal to the throttle

With the numbers

Thruster 1: |a₁| = 0.9896 > 0.8, so it stalls.
f(a₁)= −(0.8 − 1.5 × (0.9896 − 0.8)) = −(0.8 − 1.5 × 0.1896) = −(0.8 − 0.2844) = −0.5156
Thrusters 2 to 4 are within 80%, so their pushes equal their throttles: (−0.2072, −0.5951, −0.4267).
f(0.9)= 0.8 − 1.5 × (0.9 − 0.8) = 0.8 − 0.15 = 0.65
f(1)= 0.8 − 1.5 × (1 − 0.8) = 0.8 − 0.3 = 0.5

In the code the 80% point is 0.800000011920929, the computer's nearest 32-bit number to 0.8, so pushes past 80% sit 3 × 10⁻⁸ above these round numbers; at 4 decimals this changes nothing.

Chapter 1 · Step 5 of 39

1.5 What each thruster pushes

Goal: Turn the four pushes into changes of the five speed numbers.

Thruster k sits between floats k and k + 1 and adds 0.3 times its push to both of their speed numbers; 0.3 is the push factor.

A push never changes a position number directly; the swing carries it there over the next steps.

So float 1 is pushed only by thruster 1, float 5 only by thruster 4, and floats 2, 3 and 4 by two thrusters each.

A table B records which speed numbers each thruster touches: 1 where it touches, 0 elsewhere.

The rule

Float j's speed number gets 0.3 times the pushes of the thrusters on its two sides.

What the symbols mean

0.3

f(a)
the push a thruster really gives at throttle a
aj−1, aj
the throttles of the thrusters on float j's two sides (thruster j − 1 upstream of it, thruster j downstream)

There is no thruster 0 or 5; written for all floats at once with the table B.

Chapter 1 · Step 6 of 39

1.6 The water's push

Goal: Compute what the water adds to every float this step.

The water pushes every float the same way, with strength c + w₁: the current c, which never changes during an episode (one run of 100 steps, step 2.2), plus w₁, the part the wave adds right now.

Like a thruster, it adds 0.3 times its strength to each speed number, and nothing to any position number.

At start 0 the water pushes with 0.5774, so every speed number gains 0.1732 this step.

The list 𝟙speeds, with a 1 at each speed number and a 0 at each position number, writes this for all ten float numbers at once (the page's Transition Dynamics section calls this list v, a different v from the speed numbers).

The rule

Each speed number gets 0.3 times the water's push.

Chapter 1 · Step 7 of 39

1.7 The wave turns, the current stays

Goal: Turn the wave by one step and see that its size stays the same.

The two wave numbers (w₁, w₂) are a point on a circle; the circle's radius is the wave's amplitude, its largest push.

Every step the point turns by 0.27 radians around the center (a radian is a unit of angle; a full turn is 2π, about 6.283 radians), so one wave cycle takes 23.27 steps.

Turning changes the point's direction, never its distance from the center, so the amplitude stays the same.

w₁ is the push the wave adds now and w₂ the push it added a quarter of a cycle earlier. The current never changes: c′ = c, where the prime ′ means one step later.

The rule

Turn the point (w₁, w₂) by 0.27 radians; keep the current.

What the symbols mean

What the symbols mean

the two wave numbers: w₁ is the push the wave adds now, w₂ the push it added a quarter of a cycle earlier
c
the current's strength; it stays the same for a whole episode (one run of 100 steps, step 2.2)
′ (prime)
one step later: c′, w′, s′ and x′ are the next state's parts
cos 0.27, sin 0.27
the cosine and sine of the wave's turn per step, 0.963771 and 0.266731
radian
a unit of angle; a full turn is 2π, about 6.283 radians

R(θ) means: turn a pair of numbers by the angle θ.

Chapter 1 · Step 8 of 39

1.8 The floats on their own

Goal: Compute where a float would go with no thrusters and no water.

Left alone, float j's point (pⱼ, vⱼ) turns by a fixed angle θⱼ and shrinks by a fixed factor ρⱼ every step: a swing that slowly fades.

Float 1 turns 0.1 radians and shrinks by 0.98 per step; float 5 turns 0.8 radians and shrinks by 0.96, so it swings fastest and fades fastest.

A weak coupling slightly changes each float's own swing and adds small pushes from every other float; each step it adds at most 2% of the size of the ten float numbers.

The five swings and the coupling together make one fixed 10 × 10 table A; A s is where the ten float numbers go on their own.

The rule

Turn float j's point by θⱼ, then shrink it by ρⱼ.

What the symbols mean

What the symbols mean

pjown, vjown
where float j's two numbers go in one step on its own swing, before the coupling
θj, ρj
float j's turn per step, in radians, and its shrink factor per step
pj, vj
float j's position number and speed number; both are 0 when the float is at rest

The table A does all five floats at once, plus the coupling.

Chapter 1 · Step 9 of 39

1.9 One whole step: before, parts, after

Goal: Put the parts together and get all 13 numbers of the next state.

One step takes the ten float numbers to where they go on their own, plus the thrusters' part, plus the water's part.

Each speed number gets all three parts; each position number gets only the first.

The current stays, and the wave turns by 0.27 radians.

Nothing in a step is random: the same state and command always give the same next state.

The rule

Next float numbers = on their own + thrusters + water; the current stays; the wave turns.

Chapter 2. Rewards, episodes and values

Score one step, then a whole episode, then everything that follows a command.

Chapter 2 · Step 10 of 39

2.1 The reward of one step

Goal: Compute one step's reward from the state and the command.

Every step is scored by a reward, which is minus what the step costs: the best possible reward is 0, and every other reward is negative.

The float cost is the sum of the squares of the ten float numbers; it is 0 only when every float is at rest.

The throttle cost is 0.3 times the sum of the four squared throttles: the energy the thrusters use.

The throttle cost is charged on the throttle, not on the push, so a stalled thruster pays full price for a weak push.

The rule

The reward is minus (the float cost plus the throttle cost).

What the symbols mean

What the symbols mean

the reward of one step: minus the step's cost, so 0 is the best possible
‖s‖²
the float cost: the sum of the ten squared float numbers
‖a‖²
the sum of the four squared throttles
0.3
the throttle-cost weight: the weight of the squared throttles in the cost (a separate setting from the push factor, also 0.3)

The two sums of squares.

Chapter 2 · Step 11 of 39

2.2 An episode: 100 steps

Goal: Watch a controller drive a whole episode, step after step.

A controller is a rule that reads the 13 numbers and sets the four throttles; we write it π, so the command at step t is aₜ = π(xₜ).

An episode starts from a starting state and repeats the step 100 times: states 0 to 99 each get a command and a reward.

Nothing can fail, so an episode never ends early; it is simply cut off after 100 steps.

This step compares three fixed controllers (table below).

The rule

At each step t = 0, 1, …, 99 the controller picks the command, and the step of Chapter 1 gives the next state.

Chapter 2 · Step 12 of 39

2.3 Return and discounted return

Goal: Add an episode's rewards into its return, and see how a discount counts later rewards less.

The return J is the plain sum of the episode's 100 rewards: the score of the episode. Like every reward it is negative, and closer to 0 is better.

Learning methods use a second sum, the discounted return Jγ, so that nearer rewards count more and a sum with no last step (step 2.4) stays finite: a reward t steps ahead counts γᵗ times as much as one now, with the discount γ = 0.98.

A reward 10 steps ahead counts 0.82, one 35 steps ahead about half (0.49), and the last one, 99 steps ahead, 0.14.

The rule

The return adds the 100 rewards; the discounted return weighs the reward t steps ahead by γᵗ.

Chapter 2 · Step 13 of 39

2.4 The value of a command

Goal: Know what a value is, and compute one exactly.

The value of a command is the discounted sum of all the rewards that follow it, with no last step: give command a in state x, then let a controller π drive on forever.

We write it Qπ(x, a); when the first command is π's own, we write Vπ(x).

The physics has no randomness, so a value can be computed exactly by simulation; after 1,000 steps what is left is at most 8.4 × 10⁻⁸ times the largest single-step cost.

Learning methods try to estimate exactly this kind of number from recorded data alone (Chapter 4).

The rule

r₀ is the reward of command a at x; r₁, r₂, … follow π's own commands, forever.

What the symbols mean

What the symbols mean

Qπ(x, a)
the value of giving command a at state x and then letting controller π drive forever
Vπ(x)
the value of letting π drive from x: Qπ(x, π(x))
r0, r1, …
the rewards that follow: r₀ for command a at x, then π's own commands
γ
the discount, 0.98: a reward one step later counts 0.98 times as much
π
a controller: a rule that reads the 13 numbers and sets the four throttles

after step 99:−12.7275 − (−12.0934) ≈ −0.6342 (what the steps after the 100-step episode add)
No throttle from start 0: Vπ = −154.3109.
Why 1,000 steps are enough: the weights of all the steps after them add up to 0.98¹⁰⁰⁰ / (1 − 0.98) = 1.68 × 10⁻⁹ / 0.02 = 8.4 × 10⁻⁸, so what is left is at most 8.4 × 10⁻⁸ times the largest step cost.

Chapter 2 · Step 14 of 39

2.5 Why pushing past 80% is a bad trade

Goal: See that the stall's price shows only in the steps after the command.

A push past 80% can always be had more cheaply: at 90% a thruster pushes 0.65 and pays 0.243, while a throttle of 65% gives the same push for 0.127.

Compare two first commands at start 0 that differ only in thruster 1: Chapter 1's command (thruster 1 at 98.96% upstream) and the same with thruster 1 at 80%; the stall-aware controller drives afterwards.

This step's reward is lower by 0.1018, all of it throttle cost: the reward cannot see that the stalled thruster pushed less.

The weaker push lets the floats drift, which costs more later, and the values show the whole price: the full-throttle command's value is 0.3380 lower.

In the no-stall world the same command is slightly better (by 0.0222), because there its push keeps rising.

The rule

π is the stall-aware controller; afull is Chapter 1's command, a80% the same with thruster 1 at 80%.

Chapter 3. The recording, the removal and the tests

Meet the data the learner gets, follow one real row through it, and see what the main test takes out.

Chapter 3 · Step 15 of 39

3.1 The recording controller

Goal: See how the controller that made the data chooses a command, and recognize Chapter 1's command.

The learners on this page, methods that build a controller from recorded data, never drive the channel themselves: everything they learn comes from a recording made by one fixed controller, the recording controller.

Most of the time it drives normally, with a textbook rule K of 4 × 13 numbers (the best rule of its kind if the push always equaled the throttle), damping the floats only a quarter as hard as K would and adding random noise.

It then squashes each throttle with 0.8 tanh(u / 0.8); tanh is an S-shaped curve that stays between −1 and 1, so normal driving never passes 80%.

Where the water pushes harder than 0.565 (the full-throttle region), a coin flipped in each state picks, when it falls below 0.5, the full-throttle command instead: a fixed pattern P with thruster 1 at full throttle upstream, plus a little noise.

At start 0 the water pushes 0.5774 and the coin showed 0.4288, so the full-throttle command was given: the command you followed through Chapter 1.

The rule

Normal driving: e = (c, w₁, w₂) is the water part of the state; noise is four random numbers.

Chapter 3 · Step 16 of 39

3.2 One recorded row: row 209

Goal: Read a real recorded row and check it with what you already know.

A recording runs the recording controller for 1,000 episodes of 100 steps in the stalling world; each step becomes one row: the state x, the command a, the reward r and the next state x′.

Learning a controller from such a fixed recording, without ever trying a command, is called offline reinforcement learning: the learner cannot check what a command does if the recording does not contain it.

Each recording is fixed by its data seed, a number that fixes every random draw; this lesson follows data seed 0, the first of the five recordings the main test used.

The episodes are split three ways: 500 for training, 200 for calibration (rows never trained on, kept to measure errors honestly) and 300 held out for testing.

This lesson follows one real row: row 209 (episode 2, step 9), the first full-throttle row of the training episodes.

The rule

A row holds a state, its command, the reward and the next state, all made by the rules of Chapters 1 and 2.

Chapter 3 · Step 17 of 39

3.3 The removal: the commands past 80% disappear

Goal: Decide by arithmetic whether a recorded row is deleted.

The main test asks whether hiding the stall from a learner harms it, and it hides the stall by deleting training rows.

Think of each recorded command as a point with four coordinates; the test finds the smallest ball that holds 15% of the training commands and deletes every training row, and every one of the 1,000 calibration rows BCA later uses (step 3.2), whose command lies inside it.

In this recording that ball sits on the full-throttle commands, so it takes 99.49% of them: almost every row that showed what happens past 80%.

The states stay covered, because the same kinds of states keep their normal-driving rows. The page also calls the deleted region the gap.

The rule

A training row is deleted exactly when its command lies within 0.2711 of the ball's center.

the center of the deleted ball: a point with four coordinates, one per thruster

thruster k's throttle, for k = 1 to 4
⟺

Chapter 3 · Step 18 of 39

3.4 Four test situations

Goal: See how one start becomes four, and what outside the recorded conditions means.

A learned controller is tested in four situations, each with its own fixed bank of 1,000 starts (table below).

The recorded conditions use the recording's own ranges; each of the other three changes one setting: strong current, big waves or big starting pushes.

Start 0 of every bank uses the same random draws put through that situation's ranges, so start 0 in strong current is start 0 with a stronger current.

A state is outside the recorded conditions if its current is above 0.7, its wave amplitude above 0.4, or its floats are farther from the average recorded floats than 99% of the training states are (a standardized distance: each float number is first divided by its spread in the training rows); testing there is called testing out of distribution.

Strong current is the main test's key situation: holding there asks thruster 1 for 80% or more in most states, exactly the commands the removal took.

The rule

3.5 Points: one scale per situation

Goal: Turn an average return into points.

A return on its own is hard to judge, because each situation has its own scale.

Points place a controller's average return over a situation's 1,000 starts between two references: the recording controller's average is 0 points and the stall-aware controller's is 100.

100 is a reference level, not the best possible: a controller can score more.

One point is worth 0.53 units of return in the recorded conditions and 1.50 in strong current.

The rule

J is the controller's average return; Jrec and Jtop are the recording controller's and the stall-aware controller's.

Chapter 4 · Step 20 of 39

4.1 One step plus the rest: the Bellman rule

Goal: Split a value into one step and the rest, and check it with real numbers.

A value can be split into the first step and everything after it: the first reward, plus γ times the value of the state you land in.

This is the Bellman rule, named after the mathematician Richard Bellman; it holds exactly for true values, at every state and for every controller.

Check it at start 0 with the stall-aware controller.

The rule

The value of command a = its reward + 0.98 × the value of the next state.

What the symbols mean

x′

Chapter 4 · Step 21 of 39

4.2 The critic and its one-step target

Goal: Compute the critic's one-step target and its one-step error at row 209.

The learner has no simulator, only rows, so it learns a critic: a network (an adjustable function with many internal numbers, fitted to data) that estimates values.

It keeps two critics, Q₁ and Q₂, and slowly averaged copies of them and of its own controller, the actor (Q̄₁, Q̄₂ and π̄), so that its targets change slowly.

For each row it builds a one-step target y from the Bellman rule, using the lower of the two averaged critics so as not to overestimate.

The gap y − q, where q is the lower of the two critics at the recorded command, is the critic's one-step error.

Training also adds a little random noise ε to the next command inside the target; here ε = 0, so the arithmetic is exact.

The rule

The next command comes from the averaged actor; the target uses the lower averaged critic; q is the lower critic at the recorded command.

Chapter 4 · Step 22 of 39

4.3 How the critic learns

Goal: See what a training step lowers, and why a deleted row never counts.

The critic learns by lowering its loss: the average, over a batch of 256 randomly chosen kept rows, of the squared gaps between each of its two estimates and the target.

It repeats this 100,000 times with fresh batches; over the last 5,000 updates each critic misses its targets by about 0.17, measured as the root mean square (the square root of the average squared gap).

A deleted row is never in a batch, so nothing in the data corrects what the critic says there.

Row 209 was deleted, so it adds nothing; had it been kept, its term would have been 0.0625, about the size of a typical row's, because nearby kept rows taught the critic this neighborhood.

The rule

The average over the batch's rows i of both critics' squared gaps to the target.

Chapter 4 · Step 23 of 39

4.4 The actor: climb the critic, stay near the data

Goal: Compute the actor's two pulls at row 209's state.

The actor π is the learned controller: a network that turns the 13 numbers into four throttles; every second critic update it lowers a loss with two parts.

The first part, −λ mean Q₁(x, π(x)), rewards commands the first critic rates highly: the actor climbs the critic.

The second, the pull b, is the squared gap between the actor's command and the recorded command, averaged over the four thrusters; copying recorded commands like this is called behavior cloning.

The critic weight α (5 in the main test) sets the balance; dividing it by the critic's typical size, mean |Q₁|, keeps the balance the same however large the values are.

This critic-and-actor method is TD3+BC; its full name is in the key below, where policy is the field's word for a controller and gradient means slope.

The rule

The actor lowers this loss: minus λ times the critic's rating (so it climbs the critic) plus the pull b (so it stays near the recorded commands).

Chapter 4 · Step 24 of 39

4.5 Where the critic is wrong

Goal: Compare the critic's view of thruster 1 with the truth, past 80%.

At start 0, keep three thrusters where the actor puts them and slide thruster 1 from 0% to 100% upstream.

The critic's value keeps rising past 80%, while the true value, with the actor driving afterwards, peaks at 80% and falls.

The critic never saw what happens past 80%, because the removal took those rows, so it carries on the slope it learned below 80%: it extrapolates.

In strong current the mistake is about nine times as large: 3.16 against 0.35.

The rule

How much each says thruster 1 at 100% is better than at 80%; π is the actor.

Chapter 4 · Step 25 of 39

4.6 Why it hurts: start 0 in strong current

Goal: See the critic's mistake turn into lost return.

The actor climbs the critic, so at start 0 in strong current it asks three thrusters for more than 80%, and all three stall.

The critic rates this command 0.46 above the stall-aware controller's command, but its true value is 3.68 lower.

Over the episode the actor is past 80% on 74 of 100 steps and scores J = −229.83, against −69.45 for the stall-aware controller.

To measure the harm cleanly, the main test froze two critics, one learned from every row and one learned after the removal, and trained fresh actors against each, all from the same cloned actor (an actor fitted only to copy the recorded commands): the critics no longer change, so any difference in return comes from the critic.

Its frozen critics were fixed-controller critics, learned with TD3+BC's critic update while the controller they score was held fixed at the stall-aware controller: the actors trained against the one learned after the removal scored 98.9 points less in strong current.

The rule

How much better each says the actor's command is than the stall-aware controller's command asa.

Chapter 4 · Step 26 of 39

4.7 Two kinds of critic error

Goal: Tell apart the error that rows can show from the error that steers the actor.

The critic can be wrong in two different ways.

Its one-step error, y − q, compares it with itself one step later: a recorded row is enough to measure it.

Its preference error compares how it ranks two commands with how the true values rank them: measuring it needs a simulator.

At start 0 in the recorded conditions both are small; in strong current the one-step error is −1.63 (size 1.63), but the preference error is 4.14 and points the wrong way.

The method of the next chapter is built on the first kind.

The rule

The first needs only a row; the second needs the true values.

Chapter 5. BCA: a calibrated band on the critic's error

Bayesian Conformal Aggregation (BCA), the method this page tests, puts a band around the critic's value, wide where one-step errors tend to be large. Every ThrusterChain number in this chapter comes from BCA's own band, fitted on the critic of Chapter 4 in a later follow-up (step 7.2), so these numbers are exploratory: they suggest rather than prove.

Chapter 5 · Step 27 of 39

5.1 Errors on rows the critic never trained on

Goal: Turn one-step errors into scores that can be compared.

BCA, short for Bayesian Conformal Aggregation, is the method this page tests: it puts a band around the critic's value that should contain the critic's one-step error a stated share of the time, here 90%.

It measures the one-step error on the calibration rows: 5 rows from each of the 200 calibration episodes, never trained on, of which 851 survive the removal.

A small second network, the error-size network, predicts how large the error typically is at each row, g(x, a), as a multiple of a running unit η: the typical size of the critic's recent one-step errors (here 0.1676).

A row's score z is its error divided by η g: a score of 1 means the error was exactly as large as predicted, 2 means twice as large.

Row 209 is a training row and was deleted, so it is not among them, but its score works the same way: 0.814 with ε = 0 (BCA's own scores each used one random target-noise draw, as in step 4.2).

The rule

The score of calibration row i: its one-step error's size over the predicted size.

5.2 The empirical threshold

Goal: Find the score that 90% of the calibration scores do not exceed.

Sort the n scores from smallest to largest.

The empirical threshold βemp is the score at rank ⌈0.9 n⌉, where ⌈·⌉ means round up: at least 90% of the scores lie at or below it.

A band of βemp times the predicted size would have contained the error on 90% of the calibration rows; it does not yet say how sure we can be with only n rows.

Chapter 5 · Step 29 of 39

5.3 One Bayesian bootstrap draw

Goal: Do one random re-weighting of the calibration rows, and find where it crosses 90%.

βemp fits these rows, but a new row could be worse than all of them, so BCA asks which 90% thresholds are plausible by re-weighting the rows at random many times; each re-weighting is one draw of a Bayesian bootstrap.

In one draw every row gets a random positive weight E, a standard exponential random number (always positive, 1 on average), and one extra, unseen row gets one too: it stands for a new row that might be worse than all of them.

Dividing each weight by the total turns the weights into masses that add up to 1.

Walk up the sorted scores adding their masses: the draw crosses at the first score where the running total reaches 0.9. If the unseen row alone holds more than 0.1, the draw can never cross.

The rule

Row i's share of one draw's total weight.

Chapter 5 · Step 30 of 39

5.4 The credible threshold, and BCA's β

Goal: Turn 1,000 draws into a threshold and choose BCA's β.

One draw is one plausible version of how the scores are spread.

BCA makes 1,000 draws, sorts their crossings and takes the 950th smallest, so at least 95% of the draws cross at or below it: this is the credible threshold βcred.

A draw that never crosses counts as +∞ (infinity); if fewer than 950 of the 1,000 draws cross, βcred = +∞ and BCA cannot certify a band.

BCA keeps the larger of the two thresholds, β = max(βemp, βcred). Now the name makes sense: conformal is the empirical threshold on held-out rows, Bayesian is the credible threshold from the draws, and aggregation is keeping the larger.

The rule

+∞ if fewer than 950 draws cross.

Chapter 5 · Step 31 of 39

5.5 Why BCA needs at least 29 rows

Goal: See why a calibration set can be too small to certify a band.

A draw can cross only if the unseen row holds at most 10% of the mass.

Dividing the n + 1 random weights by their total is like cutting a stick of length 1 at n random points: every piece has the same chance of being long, so the unseen row's share is like the first piece, which is longer than 0.1 only if all n cuts land beyond 0.1, with probability 0.9 × 0.9 × … = 0.9ⁿ; so a draw can cross with probability 1 − 0.9ⁿ.

BCA needs 95% of its draws to cross, so it needs 1 − 0.9ⁿ ≥ 0.95: at least 29 rows.

With exactly 1,000 random draws the number that cross is itself random, so BCA's code asks for at least 36 rows, where falling short is practically impossible.

With too few rows β = +∞: BCA refuses to give a band.

The rule

Pr means probability.

BCA's own 1,000 draws on them: 852 crossed, 950 were needed, so β = +∞.
29 scores: 948 crossed, 2 short of 950. With 29 rows each draw crosses with probability 0.9529, and the chance that at least 950 of 1,000 draws cross is 0.6999 (binomial arithmetic: it adds up the chances of every count from 950 to 1,000), so 29 rows fall short 1 − 0.6999 = 30% of the time.
36 scores: 972 crossed: certified.
It happened on ThrusterChain: in the restructured BCA's step 1 (a later follow-up, step 7.2), the full-throttle group of no-stall seed 3 had exactly 29 rows, and 947 of 1,000 draws crossed (Toy worlds: what it means for ThrusterChain).

5.6 BCA's band

Goal: Compute the band's half-width at a row, and check whether an error lies inside.

BCA's band around the critic's value is q ± U, with half-width U = β η g(x, a): the threshold, times the running unit, times the predicted size at that row (the page calls U the band's width).

About 92% of one-step errors on new rows like the calibration rows fall inside it (step 5.4).

At row 209 the band is ±0.3202, and the row's one-step error, 0.1872, lies inside.

A wide band warns that the critic may be wrong there.

Chapter 6. Using the band: caution and weights

BCA turns its band into caution in one of two ways; and when the test's water is known to differ from the data's, it can weight its rows.

Chapter 6 · Step 33 of 39

6.1 Caution, first use: a harder pull

Goal: Turn the band's half-width into BCA's dose on the pull.

BCA's published way to use the band is a dose m: a multiplier on TD3+BC's pull toward the recorded command, at each training row.

Where the band is wider the pull is harder, but it never reaches 1.5 times TD3+BC's own pull.

This kind of caution, pulling the actor toward the recording, is called a behavior constraint.

Had row 209 been kept, its dose would have been 1.3282.

The rule

The dose at training row i, from 1 up to (never reaching) 1.5.

Chapter 6 · Step 34 of 39

6.2 Caution, second use: the lower edge

Goal: Compute the lower-edge penalty, and see where BCA's band cannot help.

The band's other use is its lower edge, the critic's value minus the half-width U.

In the actor's training it lowers the value of the actor's own command by [U(x, π(x)) − U(x, a)]₊, the extra width at the actor's command over the recorded one, where [v]₊ keeps v if it is positive and gives 0 otherwise. This is called value pessimism: caution on the value instead of on the command.

BCA compares the two commands at the same state, so only a command that is less certain than the recorded one is lowered.

At row 209 the band is narrower at the actor's command than at the recorded one, so the penalty is 0.

At start 0 in strong current the band's half-width is 0.4835 at the actor's stalled command and 0.4904 at the stall-aware command: it does not single out the harmful command.

The rule

The critic's value of the actor's command, lowered by the extra width there.

Chapter 6 · Step 35 of 39

6.3 Weights under a known shift

Goal: Compute a calibration row's weight from its current, when the shift is known.

Sometimes the way the test will differ from the data is known exactly: here, how often each current appears.

The page's second test, the weighting test, has its own recording, with currents from 0.1 to 1.1; its strong test meets strong currents more often than its training did.

Each calibration row then gets a weight ω(c): how many times more often its current appears at the test than in training.

Under the strong test ω(c) = exp(4 (c − 0.6)): exactly 1 at c = 0.6, from 0.14 at the weakest current to 7.39 at the strongest.

Uneven weights shrink the evidence: under the strong test 1,000 weighted rows are worth about 352 equally weighted rows.

The rule

How much more often current c appears at the test than in training.

Chapter 6 · Step 36 of 39

6.4 The weighted threshold, and refusing a step

Goal: See how weights move the threshold, and when BCA refuses a test step.

Weights change the threshold in two ways.

In each draw, every calibration row's random weight is multiplied by its ω, so rows whose currents are common at the test count more.

The unseen test step joins each draw with its own weight ω(ctest): a step whose current is rare in training takes a large share of the mass and makes crossing harder.

Past a limit fewer than 950 draws cross, β = +∞, and BCA refuses that step.

The 40 rows in the table below are an illustration, not ThrusterChain data: 40 currents drawn from the training mix, each row's score the size of (0.05 + 0.25 c) times a standard normal number (numpy's generator seeded with 20261015 and 3), and BCA's own function making the 1,000 draws (seeded with 20261015 and 1).

Each row's random weight is multiplied by its ω; so is the unseen test step's.

Chapter 7. What the tests found

Which results were fixed in advance, which came later, and the whole chain in one table.

Chapter 7 · Step 37 of 39

7.1 What the main test found

Goal: Read the main test's three checks, and why it stopped before BCA ran.

Every rule and pass mark of the main test was written down before any learner ran and locked with a fingerprint (a short code computed from the text, which changes if any character changes): it was pre-registered, so the outcome was decided by rules fixed in advance.

Check 1, is the critic wrong where data are missing: passed. It compared critics that score the fixed stall-aware controller, whose exact values are known: the one learned after the removal was 2.27 times as wrong at the removed commands as the one learned from every row (in median advantage error: the typical error in judging how much better a command is than the controller's own), and not more wrong far from them (0.75 times).

Check 2, does acting on that error cost return: passed at critic weight 5, with 98.9 points lost in strong current by fresh actors trained against the frozen critic learned after the removal (step 4.6); at 2.5 one rule failed by a hair (1.46 against 1.5).

Check 3, could caution of BCA's kind help if it were placed perfectly, by the exact over-preference (how much more the critic prefers the actor's command over the recorded one than the truth does): no. Fresh actors trained against one frozen critic, a plain TD3+BC run's critic learned after the removal, scored 1.9 points less in strong current with that caution than with the same strength spread evenly, where +3 was required.

By its own rule the test then stopped, before any BCA run.

The rule

Check 3's pass mark, needed against every control in at least one shifted situation.

What the symbols mean

3 points

With the numbers

Check 1: the error ratio at the removed commands is 2.27 (seeds 2.15 to 2.40); at least 2 was needed: passed.
Check 2: 98.9 points lost in strong current (at least 5 needed).
check 2, share of visited states past 80%: actor of the removal critic / actor of the full-recording critic:0.7316 / 0.4143 = 1.77 (at least 1.5 needed: passed at critic weight 5)
At critic weight 2.5 the same ratio was 1.46: that weight failed, so the step-up rule (fixed in advance: if critic weight 2.5 failed, the check ran again at 5, then at 10) moved to 5.
Check 3, strong current: harm-placed caution minus strength-matched even caution (one dose on every row, tuned before any return so that it moves the actor exactly as much) = −1.9; minus amount-matched caution (every row gets the average harm-placed dose, so the total extra pull is the same) = −0.6; minus shuffled doses (the same doses in a random row order) = −0.6; +3 needed: failed.
The stop: "the pre-registered rule stopped the test before any BCA run (12 Oct 2026, 20:39 UTC)".

Chapter 7 · Step 38 of 39

7.2 What the follow-ups found

Goal: Know what later work found about where caution can reach this harm.

After the stop, exploratory work (designed after seeing results, so it suggests rather than proves) asked which kind of caution can reach a harm that lies outside the data.

Stage 1, a first follow-up without BCA: a penalty on the critic's value at the actor's own command, set from the exact one-step error, won back 93.9 of the 98.9 points.

Stage 2, a second follow-up, used BCA's lower edge with a learned extra width (seeds 0 to 4): it won back 39.2 points, while a hand-set limit to the recorded range of commands won back 107.4; its confirmatory run on fresh seeds 5 to 9 has not run yet.

A restructured BCA, a version that checks the critic's errors next to the deleted commands instead of how far a command lies from the data, switched its caution on in 5 of 5 stalling-world seeds and off in 5 of 5 no-stall seeds.

The weighting test (pre-registered) found that weights restore the band's coverage under its strong test; whether weighting raises return could not be tested under its rules.

The rule

Against the 98.9 points the main test measured.

Where it stands: the project owner approved Stage 2's confirmatory run on fresh seeds 5 to 9 at their own terminal on 15 Oct 2026, 15:45 UTC, and the approval was checked against the repository's history and recorded on 16 Oct 2026, 02:27 UTC; later that day the run's plan (version 7) was ended without running, so those seeds will not run under it. Nothing has run on those seeds. So far only TD3+BC has run with BCA on ThrusterChain: the repository's other three learners that come with a BCA version, implicit Q-learning (IQL), conservative Q-learning (CQL) and revisited behavior-regularized actor-critic (ReBRAC), have not been run here (experiments/shift/learners.py imports only algorithms/td3_bc and algorithms/td3_bc_bca).
